summary: Specifies a minimum set of requirements for Internet resource locators, which convey location and access information for resources. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1736 is a checklist for designing an Internet address. It says what an address must be able to do: work the same for everyone, be understood by software or by a person, survive being written down and read back, and say only where something is and how to reach it, nothing more.

questions: what is an internet resource locator
what is the difference between a locator and a name
what must a resource locator be able to do
subtitle: The minimum properties a web address must have to work anywhere on the Internet.

tldr.problem: Every new way of pointing at a resource on the network was inventing its own idea of what an address should look like, and the differences made them hard to move between systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1736 defines a general resource locator as an object that describes the location of a resource, then lists nine properties that an Internet resource locator must have, from being transient and globally scoped to being made of a service plus an opaque parameter package.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard of any kind, and it deliberately rejects several uniqueness requirements. Its Security Considerations section sets out two ways in which a locator can be turned against the user.

facts.label: Author
facts.value: John A. Kunze, IS&T, UC Berkeley

facts.label: Drafted at
facts.value: The November 1993 IETF meeting in Houston, Texas

today: RFC 1736 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard of any kind, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It lists the minimum properties an Internet resource locator must have, and its Security Considerations section sets out two ways in which a locator can be turned against the user, because a locator is only a promise about where something was.

sections.title: What a Resource Locator Is
sections.content:
The document specifies a minimum set of requirements for Internet resource locators, which convey location and access information for resources. Typical examples of resources include network accessible documents, WAIS databases, FTP servers and Telnet destinations. Locators may also apply to resources that are not always, or not ever, network accessible; the examples given are human beings and physical objects that have no electronic instantiation, that is, objects without an existence completely defined by digital objects such as disk files.

The memo is careful to place a locator among other kinds of identifier. A resource locator is a kind of resource identifier. Other kinds allow names and descriptions to be associated with resources. A resource name is intended to provide a stable handle to refer to a resource long after the resource itself has moved, or perhaps gone out of existence. A resource description comprises a body of meta-information to assist resource search and selection.

An Internet resource locator, then, is a locator defined by an Internet resource location standard. A resource location standard, in conjunction with resource description and resource naming standards, specifies a comprehensive infrastructure for network based information dissemination. The mechanisms for mapping between locators, names and descriptive identifiers are beyond the scope of the document.

The memo also frames the problem. Network-based information resource providers require a method of describing the location of and access to their resources, and information systems users require a method whereby client software can interpret resource access and location descriptions on their behalf in a relatively transparent way. Without such a method, transparent and widely distributed, open information access on the Internet would be difficult if not impossible.
sections.plainLanguage: A locator is one of three ways of pointing at something. A name is meant to keep working for ever. A description is a pile of information meant for searching. A locator says where the thing is now, and it is expected to go out of date.

sections.title: The General Resource Locator
sections.content:
The requirements impose restrictions on the general resource locator, and the memo gives a very wide definition first, so that the contrast is clear: a general resource locator is an object that describes the location of a resource. The definition deliberately allows many degrees of freedom in order to contain the furthest reaches of the debate on resource location standards. A resource location standard shrinks the space again by applying additional requirements.

The definition has four parts, and the memo takes them one at a time. First, a general resource locator is an object. It could be a complex data structure, a contiguous sequence of bytes, a pair of latitude-longitude coordinates, a three-color road map printed on paper, or a sequence of characters that are capable of being printed on paper.

Second, it describes. In the fully general case there are many ways a locator could describe the location. It could employ a graphical or natural language description, could be heavily encoded or compressed, or could be lightly encoded and readily understandable by human beings. The description could be a multi-level hierarchy with common semantics at each level, or a multi-level hierarchy with common semantics at only the first two levels, where the semantics below the second level depend on the value given at the first level.

Third, it describes the location of something, and here the memo draws the line that matters: a resource locator describes a location but never guarantees that access may be established. While access is often desired when clients follow the location instructions given in a conformant locator, the resource need not exist any longer, or need not exist yet. Indeed it may never exist, even though the locator continues to describe a location where a resource might exist, for example when it is used as a placeholder with resource availability contingent upon an event such as a payment. The nature of certain potential resources, especially animate beings or physical objects with no electronic instantiation, makes network access meaningless in some cases; such resources have locators that would imply non-networked access, but again access is not guaranteed.

Fourth, it describes the location of a resource, and a resource can be many things: besides the non-networked or non-electronic resources just mentioned, familiar examples are an electronic document, an image, a server such as an FTP, Gopher, Telnet or HTTP server, or a collection of items such as a Gopher menu, an FTP directory or an HTML page. Other examples accompany multi-function protocols such as Z39.50, which can perform single round trip network access, session-oriented search refinement, and index browsing.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo starts with the loosest possible definition of an address and then tightens it. The important part is that an address says where something is; it never promises that anything will be there, or that you will be allowed in, or even that the thing is a computer file.

sections.title: Producers and Interpreters of Locators
sections.content:
Central to the discussion is parsability, the ability of an agent to recognise or understand a locator in whole or in part. The memo separates the two main actions associated with locators. Resource locators are both produced and interpreted. Producers are bound by the resource location standards, which are in turn bound by the requirements listed in the memo. Interpreters are not bound by the requirements; they are beneficiaries of them.

A locator is interpreted by interpreting agents, which may be human beings or software, and one or more may be employed along the way to establishing access. Several examples of multiple interpreters processing a single locator illustrate the concept that a locator may be understandable only in part by each of several interpreters but in its entirety by a combination of them. In the first example a software interpreter recognises enough of a locator to understand to which external agent it needs to be forwarded: the external agent might be a user and the locator a library call number, in which case the software forwards it simply by displaying it; or the agent might be a network software layer specialising in a particular communications protocol, in which case the service is recognised and the locator forwarded to it with an access request. In another example a human interpreter recognises enough of a locator to know where to forward it: the person might be a user who recognises a library call number as such but does not understand the location information encoded in it, and forwards it to a library employee who knows how to establish access.

A prerequisite to interpreting a locator is understanding when an object in question actually is a locator, or contains one or more locators. Some constrained environments make this easy, for example within HTML anchors or Gopher menu items. Less constrained environments, such as within running text, make it more difficult to answer without well-defined assumptions, and a resource location standard needs to make any such assumptions explicit.

On the producing side, the provider of a resource may produce a locator for it and leave the locator in places where it is intended to be discovered, such as an HTML page, a Gopher menu, or an announcement to an e-mail list. Non-providers of resources can be major producers: Web client software produces locators by translating foreign locators, such as Gopher menu items, into its own format, and locator databases such as Archie have been maintained by automated processes that produce locators for hundreds of thousands of FTP resources they discover on the Internet.

Users are major producers too. A user constructing a locator to share with others is responsible for conformance with the locator standards. Sometimes a user composes a locator on an educated guess and submits it to client software with the intent of establishing access; such a user is a producer in a sense, but if the locator is purely for personal consumption the user is not bound by the requirements. In fact some client software offers as a service to translate abbreviated, non-conformant locators entered by users into successful access instructions or into conformant locators, for example by adding a domain name to an unqualified hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: Somebody makes addresses and other people follow them, and only the makers are bound by the rules. A single address can also be understood in pieces by several people or programs, with each understanding a bit of it, and that is allowed.

sections.title: Uniqueness, and What Is Deliberately Left Out
sections.content:
The topic of a uniqueness requirement for resource locators has been discussed a great deal, and the memo considers four aspects of uniqueness before deliberately rejecting them as requirements. It is incumbent upon a resource location standard that takes on the topic to be clear about which aspects it addresses.

The first is uniqueness and multiple copies of a resource: a requirement might dictate that no identical copies of a resource may exist, and the memo makes no such requirement. The second is uniqueness and deterministic access: a requirement might dictate that the same resource accessed in one attempt will also be the result of any other successful attempt. The memo makes no such requirement, nor does it define sameness, and says it is inappropriate for a resource location standard to define sameness among resources.

The third is uniqueness and multiple locators: a requirement might dictate that a resource have no more than one locator unless all such locators are the same. The memo makes no such requirement, nor does it define sameness among locators, which a standard might do using, for example, canonicalization rules. The fourth is uniqueness, ambiguity, and multiple objects per access: a requirement might dictate that a resource locator identify exactly one object as opposed to several objects, and the memo makes no general definition of what constitutes one object, several objects, or one object consisting of several objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo spends a section on what an address is not required to do. It need not be unique: the same document may be copied, and may be given several addresses. It does not even define when two documents count as the same document.

sections.title: The Requirements List
sections.content:
The list of requirements is applied to the set of general locators, and the resulting subset, called Internet locators, is suitable for further refinement by an Internet resource location standard. Some requirements concern locator encoding while others concern locator function. One requirement from the original draft list was dropped after extensive discussion revealed it to be impractical to meet: it stated that with a high degree of reliability, software can recognise Internet locators in certain relatively unstructured environments, such as within running ASCII text.

The requirements are these. Locators are transient: the probability with which a given Internet resource locator leads to successful access decreases over time, and the more stable identifier schemes are addressed in resource naming standards, outside the scope of a resource location standard. Locators have global scope: the name space of resource locators includes the entire world, and the probability of successful access using an Internet locator depends in no way, modulo resource availability, on the geographical or Internet location of the client.

Locators are parsable: Internet locators can be broken down into complete constituent parts sufficient for interpreters, software or human, to attempt access if desired. These requirements do not bind interpreters, but three points bear emphasising. A given kind of locator may still be parsable even if a given interpreter cannot parse it. Parsable by users does not imply readily parsable by untrained users. And a given locator need not be completely parsable by any one interpreter as long as a combination of interpreters can parse it completely.

Locators can be readily distinguished from naming and descriptive identifiers that may occupy the same name space, because during a transition period, of possibly indefinite length, other kinds of resource identifier are expected to co-exist in data structures along with Internet locators.

Locators are transport-friendly: they can be transmitted from user to user, for example by electronic mail, across Internet standard communications protocols without loss or corruption of information. And locators are human transcribable: users can copy them from one medium to another, such as voice to paper, or paper to keyboard, without loss or corruption of information, and the process is not required to be comfortable.

An Internet locator consists of a service and an opaque parameter package. The parameter package has meaning only to the service with which it is paired, where a service is an abstract access method, which might be a software tool, an institution, or a network protocol, and the parameter package might be service-specific access instructions. In order to protect creative development of new services, there is an extensible class of services for which no parameter package semantics common across services may be assumed.

The set of services is extensible, since new services can be added over time. And locators contain no information about the resource other than that required by the access mechanism: the purpose of an Internet locator is only to describe the location of a resource, not other properties such as its type, size or modification date, and those belong in a resource description standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the checklist. An address should be short-lived, should mean the same thing wherever you are, should be understandable in parts, should be easy to tell apart from names and descriptions, should survive being mailed or read aloud, and should be made of a service plus whatever that service needs to do its job.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conclusion
sections.content:
The requirements have no direct security implications, but applications based on standards that fulfil them may need to consider two potential vulnerabilities. The first is that, because locators are transient, a client using an invalid locator might unwittingly gain access to a resource that was not the intended target. The example given is a hostname that becomes unregistered for a period of time and then is registered again, where a locator that was no longer valid during that period might once again lead to a resource, but perhaps to one that only pretends to be the original resource.

The second vulnerability comes from the service and parameter package structure, because potentially enormous processing freedom is allowed depending on the individual service. A server is vulnerable unless it suitably restricts its input parameters; for example, a server that advertises locators for certain local filesystem objects may inadvertently open a door through which other filesystem objects can be accessed. A client is also vulnerable unless it understands the limitations of the service it is using, for example a client trusting a locator obtained from an uncertain source might inadvertently trigger a mechanism that applies charges to a user account, and a clear definition of service limitations could help alleviate this.

For services that by nature offer a great deal of user freedom, remote login being the example, the pre-specification of user commands within a locator presents vulnerabilities. With careful command screening, the deleterious effects of unknowingly executing, at the client or the server, an embedded command such as rm -fr * can be avoided.

The conclusion restates the case. Resource location standards give providers the means to describe access information for their resources, and give client developers the ability to access disparate resources while hiding access details from users. Several minimum requirements distinguish an Internet locator from a general one: Internet resource locators are impermanent handles sufficiently qualified for resource access not to depend in general on client location; they can be recognised and parsed; and they can be transmitted unscathed through a variety of human and Internet communication mechanisms. An Internet resource locator consists of a service and access parameters meaningful to that service, and the form of the locator does not discourage the addition of new services or the migration to other resource identifiers. A clean distinction between resource location, resource naming and resource description standards is preserved by limiting Internet locators to no more information than what is required by an access mechanism.

The core requirements arose from a collaboration at the November 1993 IETF meeting in Houston, Texas, and the memo lists the people involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Two dangers follow from the design. An address that has gone stale can quietly lead somewhere else. And because the part after the service name is opaque, a server that hands out addresses without checking what they ask for can be walked through, so the memo ends by asking servers to screen the commands embedded in addresses.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF THE DEFINITION OF A LOCATOR

cells: An object
A complex data structure, a contiguous sequence of bytes, a pair of latitude-longitude coordinates, a three-color road map printed on paper, or characters printable on paper.
That describes
A graphical or natural language description, heavily encoded or compressed, or lightly encoded and readily understandable by human beings.
The location of
A location, but never a guarantee that access can be established, or that anything will ever be there.
A resource
An electronic document, an image, a server such as FTP, Gopher, Telnet or HTTP, or a collection of items such as a Gopher menu or an HTML page.

viz.caption: THE NINE REQUIREMENTS FOR AN INTERNET RESOURCE LOCATOR

cells: Transient
The chance that a locator leads to successful access decreases over time; stable identifiers belong to resource naming standards.
Global scope
The name space covers the whole world, and success does not depend on where the client is.
Parsable
Broken into complete parts enough for an interpreter to try; several interpreters together may parse what one cannot.
Distinguishable
Readily told apart from naming and descriptive identifiers sharing the same name space.
Transport-friendly
Transmitted from user to user across Internet standard protocols without loss or corruption.
Human transcribable
Copied from one medium to another, voice to paper or paper to keyboard, without loss or corruption.
Service plus opaque parameters
The parameter package means something only to the service it is paired with.
Extensible services
New services can be added over time.
No extra information
Nothing about the resource beyond what the access mechanism requires; type, size and dates belong to description standards.

viz.caption: THE WAYS A LOCATOR CAN GO WRONG

items.title: The stale address
items.text: Because locators are transient, a client using an invalid locator might unwittingly reach a resource that was not the intended target, such as when a hostname is unregistered and then registered again.

items.title: Unrestricted parameters
items.text: A server is vulnerable unless it restricts its input parameters, and a client is vulnerable unless it understands the limits of the service it is using.

items.title: Embedded commands
items.text: For services that offer a lot of user freedom, such as remote login, careful command screening avoids unknowingly running something like rm -fr *.

items.title: A dropped requirement
items.text: Software recognising locators in unstructured environments such as running ASCII text was dropped from the draft list, because it proved impractical to meet.
